extracted.intended_audience: students of literature / readers studying comparative literary criticism and poetic theory (Schlegel's lectures)
extracted.subtask_description: A study-guide/question-list for assessing poetry, fiction, and drama across national traditions and historical periods, focusing on suitable subjects, forms, styles, and the relation of literature to religion, language, and social change.

rubrics_metrics.name: True end / purpose of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the true end of poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry's fundamental purpose as a primary evaluative criterion — ask whether a poem attains its central aim (moral, imaginative, religious, national, or aesthetic). Consider how various poets and traditions define poetry's end (e.g., Christian vs. chivalric aims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate subject selection
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the proper subjects of poetry? How is the spiritual world to be treated? How the actual and present? How traditions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should choose subjects suitable to its nature: spiritual and traditional material (heroic ages, myths, legends) are often proper; the precise present and mere precision of detail tend to reduce poetic effect. Use examples (Homer, romantic/heroic subjects) to judge fitness of subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of religious / sacred material
rubrics_metrics.description: Does Christianity (or religion generally) make a proper subject for poetry? What can and cannot be directly revealed poetically?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious mysteries require cautious handling: Christianity should not be merely represented as ordinary poetic subject; it may provide groundwork or symbolism. Excessive direct revelation of mysteries often produces defects (e.g., over-obscure or didactic poetry). Consider Biblical simplicity and symbolism as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegory and symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: How does allegory influence poetry and other classes? What are the advantages and dangers of a symbolizing spirit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate degree and effect of allegory: it encourages imagination and moral depth but can be corrupted (obscurity or false mysticism). Compare Bible's symbolic spirit, medieval allegory, and later allegorical tendencies (e.g., where allegory is ground-work vs. where it predominates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and connection (coherence) of a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Are unity and connection of a poem maintained? Is the plan coherent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural unity and intelligibility (Dante's unity and plan are discussed as criteria). Excessive obscurity or requirement of commentators signals a weakness in communication. Evaluate whether plot, thematic progression, and connections are clear to intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensibility / need for commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the poem intelligible to contemporaries or does it require constant commentary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that are excessively obscure may have literary value but fail as accessible poetry. Consider whether complexity enriches or obstructs understanding (Dante's need for commentators noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: National / cultural appropriateness of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Should a nation adopt literary forms of another nation, or invent its own dramatic/poetic form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every nation must invent or adapt forms suited to its character; external forms (e.g., Spanish drama) may be unsuitable in Northern Europe. Evaluate whether a work's form fits the moral, social, and theatrical conditions of its culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of dramatic mode to fit effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Which of the three modes of tragic/dramatic conclusion is appropriate (high/serious/hybrid)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tragic/dramatic mode according to purpose and national taste: the three species (serious classical conclusion, another middle kind, and the third adapted to the modern/romantic) suit different aims. Use examples (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Shakespeare) to judge appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of dramatic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the essence of dramatic composition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge drama by its core: dramatic action, living conflict, and the representation of human passions in performance. Evaluate pacing, unity of action, and whether the drama achieves theatrical effectiveness rather than merely rhetorical or narrative excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and craft vs. rapid prolific composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Is rapidity of composition injurious to quality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid, prolific production (Lope de Vega example) can yield fertility but often sacrifices craft and depth; prefer careful composition for drama to secure unity and dramatic effect rather than sheer quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and variety of poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Should a poet be rich and various rather than uniform? Are concetti (ornamental conceits) condemned or permissible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity is excused rarely; poets should display variety and richness. Avoid excessive concetti if they produce mannerism (discussion of Tasso, Marino). Compare poets (Camoens vs. Tasso) for tenderness, variety, and concetti use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of merit for romantic/heroic fictions
rubrics_metrics.description: By what standard is the merit of romantic fictions measured? What is the essential mark of distinction between Christian fictions and all others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate romantic fictions by their imaginative scope, moral spirit, and national resonance; Christian fictions are distinguished by a particular spirit/symbolism rooted in religion. Consider historical and spiritual qualities rather than mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cultural influence on literature
rubrics_metrics.description: How have events like the Crusades, Turkish invasions, invention of the press, or discoveries affected subjects, forms, and merits of literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works in light of historical catalysts (Crusades, reformation, printing press) which change subject matter (exposure to Oriental tales), language development, and public taste. Determine whether effects are deep (altering national character) or superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and transformation of traditional material
rubrics_metrics.description: How are ancient myths, heroic cycles, and traditional machinery transmitted and transformed (e.g., Alexander legends, Trojan wars, Persian heroes)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether traditions are adapted imaginatively or merely copied; judge originality in transformation and the poet's capacity to integrate foreign material into national forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative evaluation — compare poems by their object
rubrics_metrics.description: With what should we compare poems — by rules or by their object?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer comparative standards grounded in the poem's aims and cultural object rather than rigid formal rules. Evaluate similarity of spirit and purpose when comparing works across traditions (avoid false analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language development and choice
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the state and development of a nation's language affect its literature? Which foreign languages should be studied to improve one's own?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literary works considering language maturity and purity; recognize that using foreign languages can corrupt or enrich native literature. Encourage study of select languages for improvement but avoid making a foreign tongue the vehicle of national expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in sacred writing vs. philosophical ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the Bible's striking peculiarities (simplicity and symbolic spirit) and how do these affect poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacred writings often favor simplicity and symbolic expression over ornamented philosophical style; when evaluating religious poetry, prefer simplicity that expresses moral/spiritual truth rather than excessive rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of myth and antiquity in poetic models
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent should poets adopt antique models (Virgil, Aristotle) or national myths (heroic ages)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antique models as inspiration, not slavish rules; some poets (Ariosto, Camoens) use classical models and then adapt them creatively. National myths may be preferable for patriotic/national epics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of subject to genre (lyric, epic, dramatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: What subjects best suit lyric, heroic/epic, or dramatic poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genres by their proper subjects and methods: lyric for personal emotion, epic for national/heroic narratives, drama for enacted conflicts. Evaluate whether a work aligns subject and genre effectively (Don Quixote as a questionable model, Richardson vs Spanish fiction examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of theatrical practices by national stage conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: How do theatre practices and audience conditions (Madrid, London, Paris vs Germany/Italy) affect dramatic quality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge plays by whether their form and techniques suit local theatrical conventions (Spanish theatre's early perfection owed to local conditions). A form successful in one country may fail elsewhere; analyze audience, staging, and national taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ranks/species of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Which species of drama belong to lower scales and which to higher (low comedy vs high tragic art)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify drama and judge ambition: low popular species have social value but limited artistic claim; higher drama aims at profound tragic or romantic effects (Shakespeare, classical tragedians). Evaluate according to intended rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Christian/Protestant influences on literature
rubrics_metrics.description: What has been the effect of the Reformation and religious change upon poetry, philosophy, and freedom of thought?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether religious shifts encouraged liberty of thought, altered philosophical schools (Aristotelian vs Platonic), and changed poetic themes. Evaluate writers and schools in context of religious-political background.
